title: Packet capture with Wireshark: capture and display filters

videos.script: A server is slow, and somebody says: look at the packets. {{question}} The first problem is where to look from. A switch sends each frame only to the port it is meant for. Plug a laptop into the next port and you see almost nothing. {{switch}} So the capture goes on a mirror port, which gets a copy of another port's traffic, or on the server itself. {{mirror}} The second problem is how much to keep. Wireshark has two filters for that. The capture filter decides what is saved at all, and what it drops is gone. The display filter decides what you see. It hides packets and deletes none. {{filters}} They look alike, and they are two different languages. Type one into the other's box and it fails, sometimes loudly and sometimes without a word. {{mistakes}} This lab has no screen, so you will watch everything through tshark. It is Wireshark's own engine in a terminal, and the filters are typed exactly as in the window. {{tshark}} By the end you will save a capture and ask it six questions. You will follow one conversation from the request to the page, and count who talked to whom. {{stats}}
